analysis.one_liner: Caps tax deductions from partnership land-conservation donations at 2.5 times each partner's investment.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee; it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, despite bipartisan sponsorship by Sen. Daines (R-MT) and Sen. Stabenow (D-MI) and three Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Some investors buy land through partnerships, donate a conservation easement on it, and claim a tax deduction many times larger than the money they actually put in. This bill would cap each partner's deduction at 2.5 times their investment in the partnership for the first five years, and it would not apply to family partnerships. Its goal is to keep the legitimate conservation-easement deduction from being used as a tax shelter.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, because closing inflated deductions keeps money in the Treasury. Legitimate conservation donors are left alone: the cap only applies to partnership deals in the first five years of a partner's participation, and family partnerships are exempt.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers footing the bill for inflated deductions

how_it_helps.text: Caps a partner's annual deduction for a partnership's conservation contribution at 2.5 times that partner's adjusted basis in the partnership, for the first five years after they join.
Exempts family partnerships and directs the Treasury to write rules to prevent avoidance of the cap.
Applies to contributions made after December 23, 2016, so deals structured before that date are treated under prior law.

analysis.who_pays: Syndicators who package conservation-easement deals and wealthy investors in those partnerships, whose deductions would be capped well below what current law allows them to claim.

drawbacks.text: The cap could also reduce deductions for genuine conservation contributions made through partnerships, not just abusive ones; the bill draws no line between the two beyond the 2.5-times-basis limit.
The exemption for family partnerships leaves open a planning route to structure deals within family groups outside the cap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: fewer deductions that exceed what investors actually paid in, which protects federal revenue and the credibility of a real conservation incentive. The cost falls almost entirely on the investors and promoters the cap targets. The main design weakness is that the cap is blunt — it can catch some legitimate partnership donations along with the shelters — but the family-partnership carve-out and the five-year window narrow its reach. On balance this is a targeted anti-shelter rule, not a cut to land conservation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Steve Daines introduced the bill on February 15, 2018, together with Sen. Debbie Stabenow.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history for the rest of the Congress.
The bill would have limited a partner's deduction for a partnership's conservation contribution to 2.5 times the partner's basis in the partnership during the first five years of membership.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors and promoters in syndicated conservation-easement deals kept the ability to claim deductions far beyond their actual investment, and the Treasury kept absorbing them. The bipartisan sponsors' proposal never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Steve Daines
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap partnership conservation-easement deductions.

for.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction as its Democratic co-lead.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, so it never advanced past referral.

against.name: Conservation-easement syndication industry
against.role: Promoters and investors in syndicated easement deals
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation of this kind, which would cap the deductions their deals produce, through lobbying and allied organizations.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsor co-led the bill with the top Democrat on the Senate Agriculture Committee, and its three cosponsors were all Democrats; the bill stalled in committee rather than along party lines.

industries.note: These promoters package land deals so investors can claim easement deductions many times their cost, shifting tax revenue from the public to private investors. The cap directly shrinks that business model, which is why the bill died with bipartisan sponsorship and no recorded floor opposition.

The bill leaves legitimate easement donations untouched while curbing the inflated partnership deductions that invite IRS scrutiny of the whole program. A credible deduction protects the conservation funding stream land trusts rely on.
The bill caps their deductions at 2.5 times their actual investment for their first five years in a deal. The family-partnership exemption is their main remaining planning route.
